title: Lessons from the First Statewide Mandate on School Start Times
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Aldeman reports on a new NBER study of California's SB 328, the first statewide mandate delaying middle and high school start times, which found the policy increased the share of students sleeping the CDC-recommended 8+ hours by 13%, produced measurable reductions in sadness, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation among boys, and raised eighth-grade math and English scores by roughly 0.08-0.10 standard deviations, with the largest academic gains among Hispanic and economically disadvantaged students. He notes the study corroborates its findings using a secondary measure, teachers' commute arrival times as a proxy for pre-policy start times, and finds academic gains accumulating from 2023 to 2025 alongside a suggestive decline in dropout rates. Aldeman contrasts this strong evidence base with his own district's recent experience, where 16 months of contracted study, focus groups, and a 233-page report on delaying middle school start times still ended with the school board dropping the issue, because there was no cost-free option and no unanimous community consensus. His conclusion is that later start times are a rare case in education policy where the research evidence is unusually strong and the primary barrier to adoption is logistical and political rather than a legitimate scientific dispute.
points: The NBER study's most striking finding is a genuine dose-response pattern: boys and Hispanic students, the groups experiencing the largest sleep-timing shifts, also showed the clearest reductions in sadness and suicidal ideation and difficulty concentrating, respectively.

The 0.08-0.10 standard deviation gain in 8th-grade math and English scores is corroborated by a second data source, teachers' commute arrival times as a proxy for old start times, strengthening the causal claim beyond a single before/after comparison.

Aldeman's Fairfax County anecdote, 16 months of study, a 233-page report, and broad agreement that later start times would help, yet no adopted policy, illustrates that for this issue the obstacle is logistical and political consensus, not scientific uncertainty.

He frames later start times as unusually rare in education policy: a change with real costs but evidence strong enough that the juice may be worth the squeeze, a bar few education interventions clear.
quotes: We find that SB 328 increased the share of students sleeping at least 8 hours per night by 13%, meeting the CDC-recommended minimum for this age group.

Average mental health effects are imprecisely estimated, but boys show significant reductions in sadness, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation, and Hispanic students, who experienced the largest sleep-timing shifts, show parallel reductions in difficulty concentrating.
Math and English scores in grade 8 improved by approximately 0.08-0.10 standard deviations, with the largest gains among Hispanic and economically disadvantaged students.

A within-state analysis using teachers' commute arrival times as a proxy for pre-policy school start times corroborates these findings, and shows academic gains accumulating over 2023-2025 alongside a suggestive decline in high school dropout rates.

There seemed to be broad agreement that later school start times would be better, for all the reasons you might expect: better sleep leads to better mental health and better academic outcomes. But the community wasn't unanimously behind any of the proposed alternatives, there was no solution that was cost-free, and so the School Board eventually dropped the issue.

It is true that there are costs involved with changing school start times, including adapting bus routes and sports schedules and disrupting family routines. But this study provides new evidence that the gains for students are real, and the juice may be worth the squeeze.
